(i) M(C4H10O) = 74, which matches the molecular ion peak at 74, so the molecular formula is C4H10O.

(ii) 74 − 59 = 15: loss of a CH3 group, giving the fragment C3H7O+.

(iii) O–H (alcohol, hydrogen-bonded).

Oxidation to a carboxylic acid means C is a primary alcohol:

CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (butan-1-ol) and (CH3)2CHCH2OH (2-methylpropan-1-ol).
Amino (amine) group, –NH2, and carboxylic acid group, –COOH.

Three isomers of C3H8O (full structural formulas with all H atoms shown):

  • CH3CH2CH2OH — propan-1-ol (I)
  • CH3CH(OH)CH3 — propan-2-ol (II)
  • CH3OCH2CH3 — methoxyethane (III), an ether
The spectrum is methoxyethane (III). Alcohols show a broad O–H band above 3000 cm−1 (3200–3600); the 1000–1300 cm−1 band is the C–O bond, so the compound has C–O–C but no O–H.

Spectrum A (3:2:2:1) = propan-1-ol: CH3 (3H), CH2 (2H), CH2O (2H), OH (1H) — four environments.

Spectrum B (6:1:1) = propan-2-ol: two equivalent CH3 groups (6H), CH (1H), OH (1H).

C=C (alkene): add bromine water — orange/brown colour is decolourised.

–COOH (carboxylic acid): add sodium carbonate (or hydrogencarbonate) solution — effervescence of CO2. (Na metal giving bubbles, or an acid–base indicator, also accepted.)

(i) Any three: C=C 1610–1680 cm−1; C=O 1680–1750 cm−1; C–H 2840–3095 cm−1; O–H (acid, broad) 2500–3300 cm−1.

(ii) CH3 ≈ 0.9 ppm (on a C=C the actual shift is nearer 1.7–2 ppm); C=C–H 4.9–5.9 ppm; COOH ≈ 11.5 ppm. Peak area ratio 6 : 1 : 1 (two CH3 : alkene H : COOH).

p2.key:
(i) NMR: B and C have the same functional groups, so IR spectra are very similar, but their H environments differ — B gives 5 peaks [(CH3)2, CH, CH(OH), OH, COOH] whereas C gives only 4 [(CH3)2, CH2, OH, COOH].

(ii) Basis: B is a secondary alcohol and is easily oxidised; C is a tertiary alcohol and is not. Warm with acidified potassium dichromate(VI): with B, orange → green; with C, stays orange. (Acidified KMnO4: purple → colourless with B only.)

(i) Optical activity is the ability to rotate the plane of plane-polarised light. An optically active molecule has a chiral (asymmetric) carbon — one bonded to four different groups — so it is non-superimposable on its mirror image.

(ii) B is optically active: its C bearing OH has four different groups (H, OH, COOH, CH(CH3)2). Draw the two enantiomers as 3-D tetrahedral mirror images (wedge/dash bonds) with a mirror between them. One rotates plane-polarised light clockwise (+), the other anticlockwise (−) by the same angle.

C has no chiral centre (the C–OH carbon carries two CH3 groups).

Match each absorption to the data booklet ranges:

  • A: 3400 cm⁻¹ → O–H (alcohol).
  • B: 1720 cm⁻¹ → C=O.
  • C: 1720 and 3100 cm⁻¹ → C=O and O–H (carboxylic acid, broad O–H).
  • D: 1650 cm⁻¹ → C=C.

• A: butan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (a primary alcohol, as it oxidizes to an aldehyde then acid).
  • B: butanal, CH3CH2CH2CHO.
  • C: butanoic acid, CH3CH2CH2COOH.
  • D: but-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH3.

Answers based on 2-methylpropan-1-ol (and its products) are also accepted.
Elimination (dehydration), using a catalyst of concentrated sulfuric acid or phosphoric acid (or heated Al2O3). The other product is water.

p2.key:
Feature: a chiral (asymmetric) carbon – a C atom bonded to four different atoms/groups.

Isomer of A: butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (C2 carries H, OH, CH3 and C2H5).

(i) Homologous series: same general formula; successive members differ by CH2; similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (any three). Functional group: the atom/group of atoms responsible for the characteristic reactions of the compound/series.

(ii) Ethanoic acid has the higher melting point: it has larger mass and stronger intermolecular forces (London forces and more extensive H-bonding / dimers). (H-bonding alone does not score — both have it.)

(iii) Butan-1-ol CH3CH2CH2CH2OH; butan-2-ol CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3; 2-methylpropan-1-ol (CH3)2CHCH2OH; 2-methylpropan-2-ol (CH3)3COH [2]. Butan-2-ol shows optical isomerism [1]: C2 is a chiral centre with four different groups (H, OH, CH3, C2H5) [1].

(i) II (HCOOCH=CH2) decolourises bromine (addition across C=C); I has only saturated groups, so no reaction (in the dark).

(ii) IR: II shows a C=C absorption (1610–1680 cm−1) absent in I; fingerprint regions differ.
¹H NMR: I (HCOO–CH2–CH3) has 3 peaks in ratio 1 : 2 : 3; II (HCOO–CH=CH2) has 3 peaks in ratio 1 : 1 : 2.

(iii) Addition polymerisation. Repeat unit: –[CH2–CH(OOCH)]– i.e. –CH2–CH– with an –O–CHO side group.

(i) IR absorption near 1720 cm−1 shows a C=O group in both. NMR 3 peaks in ratio 3 : 2 : 1 shows three different H environments containing 3, 2 and 1 H.
C = propanal, CH3CH2CHO; D = propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH.

(ii) D (carboxylic acid) also absorbs at 2500–3300 cm−1 (O–H in acids) and 1000–1300 cm−1 (C–O).

B is propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH (primary alcohol, since it oxidises to an aldehyde then acid) [1].

¹H NMR peak areas: 3 : 2 : 2 : 1 (CH3, CH2, CH2O, OH) [1].

Ester isomer of C3H6O2: methyl ethanoate CH3COOCH3 or ethyl methanoate HCOOCH2CH3 [1].

The ester has no O–H group [1], so it cannot form as many hydrogen bonds with water as D (which has O–H to donate and accept H-bonds) [1].

(i) Any two: same general formula (CnH2n+2); successive members differ by CH2; similar chemical properties; gradual change in physical properties; same functional group.

(ii) Hydrocarbon: a compound containing carbon and hydrogen only.

(iii) Saturated: contains only single C–C bonds (no multiple bonds).

(i) Boiling point increases as the number of carbon atoms increases [1], because larger molecules have more electrons/greater surface area, so stronger London (van der Waals') forces [1].

(ii) Combustion is exothermic: more energy is released forming the bonds in CO2 and H2O than is needed to break bonds in the alkane and O2, so products have lower enthalpy than reactants.

(i) Molecular ion peak at m/z = 74, which equals M of C3H6O2, so molecular formula = C3H6O2 (same as empirical).

(ii) m/z 45: C2H5O+ (or HCOO+/COOH+); m/z 29: C2H5+ (or CHO+). Fragments must carry + charge.

(i) No broad O–H absorption at 2500–3300 cm−1, which a carboxylic acid would show.

(ii) C–H: absorption ~2840–3095 cm−1; C=O: strong absorption ~1680–1750 cm−1; C–O: absorption ~1000–1300 cm−1. (Bond and its wavenumber evidence needed for each mark.)

HCOOCH2CH3 — ethyl methanoate (an ester: C=O and C–O but no O–H; fragments HCOO/C2H5 fit).

Use of esters: flavourings, perfumes/fragrances, solvents or plasticisers.
3 peaks [1]: H atoms are in three different chemical environments — HCOO–, –CH2–, –CH3 (ratio 1 : 2 : 3) [1].
Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas (different arrangement of atoms).
Any two other C3H6O2 structures, e.g. CH3COOCH3 (methyl ethanoate) and CH3CH2COOH (propanoic acid). Show all H atoms.

• CH3CH2CH2CH2Cl – 1-chlorobutane, primary
  • CH3CH2CHClCH3 – 2-chlorobutane, secondary
  • (CH3)2CHCH2Cl – 1-chloro-2-methylpropane, primary
  • (CH3)3CCl – 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, tertiary

[1] per formula; [4] for all names/classes. Primary/secondary/tertiary = number of C atoms bonded to the C bearing Cl (1, 2, 3). "Chlorobutane" alone is not accepted; use hyphens, not commas, between number and name.

• CH3CH2CH2OH – propan-1-ol
  • CH3CH(OH)CH3 – propan-2-ol
  • CH3CH=CH2 – propene (the dehydration product of both)

The third C3H8O isomer, methoxyethane (an ether), cannot be dehydrated to an alkene.

(i) Propene, C3H6: 3 peaks, ratio 3 : 2 : 1 (as marked). Propan-1-ol: 4 peaks, 3 : 2 : 2 : 1; or propan-2-ol: 3 peaks, 6 : 1 : 1.

(ii) C3H8O only: O–H at 3200–3600 cm−1 (or C–O at 1050–1410 cm−1). C3H6 only: C=C at 1620–1680 cm−1.

Note: strictly, the two =CH2 H atoms in propene are inequivalent, but the markscheme accepts 3 : 2 : 1.

CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3, butan-2-ol.

C2 is chiral: it carries four different groups (H, OH, CH3, C2H5), so the molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable.

Distinguish: the enantiomers rotate the plane of plane-polarized light in opposite directions (polarimeter).

Secondary: CH3CHBrCH2CH3, 2-bromobutane.

Other primary: (CH3)2CHCH2Br, 1-bromo-2-methylpropane.

• m/z 136 and 138 (equal height): molecular ions containing the two bromine isotopes, 79Br and 81Br;
  • m/z 57: C4H9+ (loss of Br);
  • m/z 42: C3H6+ (further loss of CH3);
  • this was taken as the tertiary isomer, (CH3)3CBr.

Fragments need positive charges ([−1] once if missing).

(CH3)3CH (2-methylpropane): nine equivalent H on three CH3 groups and one H on the central C → 9 : 1.
Any two: same general formula; successive members differ by CH2; same functional group; similar chemical properties; gradual trend in physical properties (e.g. b.p.).
HCOOCH3, methyl methanoate (an ester, same formula C2H4O2). Other correct isomers accepted (e.g. HOCH2CHO, 2-hydroxyethanal).

Carbon 2 is a chiral (asymmetric) carbon: it has four different groups (H, OH, CH3, C2H5), so the molecule has non-superimposable mirror images. To distinguish the enantiomers, pass plane-polarized light through each one. They rotate the plane of polarization by equal amounts in opposite directions.

(i) B is but-2-ene, CH3CH=CHCH3. It has 6 equivalent CH3 H and 2 equivalent =CH H, giving a 3:1 ratio.

(ii) C is but-1-ene, CH2=CHCH2CH3, with four H environments: 3:2:2:1 (CH3, CH2, =CH2, =CH).

Different: X (the acid) has a broad O–H at 2500–3300 cm−1; Z (the ester) has C–O at 1000–1300 cm−1 (with no O–H).

(ii) C3H6O: propanone, CH3COCH3, and propanal, CH3CH2CHO. An unsaturated or cyclic alcohol is also accepted. Show all H atoms.

(iii) Optical isomers are non-superimposable mirror images that rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. The alcohol is butan-2-ol, CH3CH2C*H(OH)CH3; the chiral carbon is C2, which carries H, OH, CH3 and C2H5.

(iv) The other three are butan-1-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol with no H on the C–OH carbon, so it is not oxidized.

(ii) Alcohol: propan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2OH. Acid: ethanoic acid, CH3COOH. In a full structural formula every H must be shown.

(i) I: ethanoic acid, CH3COOH. II: methyl methanoate, HCOOCH3. In Lewis structures show all lone pairs on the O atoms (penalized once if missing).

(ii) II (the ester) is more volatile. It has no O–H, so there is no hydrogen bonding between its molecules, only dipole–dipole forces, which are weaker than the hydrogen bonding in the acid.

(i) Pentan-3-ol, (CH3CH2)2CHOH, has 4 peaks with areas 6 : 4 : 1 : 1 (2×CH3, 2×CH2, CH, OH).

(ii) O–H at 3200–3600 cm−1; C–H at 2850–3090 cm−1; C–O at 1000–1300 cm−1. Two correct ranges score [1]; all three score [2].
Isomers are compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas (different arrangements of atoms).

(i) C3H6O: propanal CH3CH2CHO and propanone CH3COCH3. Test: warm with acidified potassium dichromate(VI). Propanal turns it from orange to green (an aldehyde is oxidized). Propanone causes no change, because ketones are not oxidized. Tollens' or Fehling's tests are also accepted.

(ii) C3H6O2: propanoic acid CH3CH2COOH and methyl ethanoate CH3COOCH3 (or ethyl methanoate HCOOC2H5). Test: add sodium carbonate (or a reactive metal). The acid gives effervescence (CO2), and the ester shows no effect. An indicator also works, e.g. blue litmus turns red for the acid only.

The result must be stated for both isomers. IR and NMR are not chemical tests.

(i) C: 85.6/12.01 = 7.13; H: 14.4/1.01 = 14.3, a ratio of 1 : 2, so the empirical formula is CH2 (14.03). 56.1/14.03 = 4, so the molecular formula is C4H8.

(ii) Methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2. Its ¹H NMR peak areas are 6 : 2 (3 : 1).

(iii) CH3CH=CHCH3, but-2-ene.

(iv) CH2=CHCH2CH3 (but-1-ene). It forms by dehydration (elimination) of butan-1-ol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (butan-2-ol is also accepted).

Butane, CH3CH2CH2CH3, has two hydrogen environments:

  • the 6 H of the two equivalent CH3 groups
  • the 4 H of the two equivalent CH2 groups

So there are 2 peaks with areas 6 : 4 = 3 : 2.

• Optical isomers have a chiral centre: a carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
  • The two enantiomers rotate the plane of plane-polarized light (measured with a polarimeter)…
  • …by equal amounts in opposite directions.

• A: CH3CH2CH2CH2OH (butan-1-ol). It is primary (gives an acid), not chiral, and has 5 H environments.
  • B: CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 (butan-2-ol). It is secondary (gives a ketone) and chiral.
  • C: (CH3)2CHCH2OH (2-methylpropan-1-ol). It is primary and has 4 H environments.
  • D: (CH3)3COH (2-methylpropan-2-ol). It is tertiary (not oxidized) and has 2 H environments.

• Draw two 3-D (wedge/dash) tetrahedral structures of butan-2-ol around the chiral C, with H, OH, CH3 and C2H5. They must be mirror images of each other.
  • CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH2CH3 + H2O
  • The product is butanone (a ketone).

• CH2=CHCH2CH3, but-1-ene (from A or B)
  • CH3CH=CHCH3, but-2-ene (from B; cis and trans forms are also accepted)
  • (CH3)2C=CH2, methylpropene (from C or D)

The IR absorptions at 1000–1300 cm−1 (C–O) and 3230–3550 cm−1 (O–H) show both are alcohols: E/F are propan-1-ol CH3CH2CH2OH and propan-2-ol CH3CH(OH)CH3. The third isomer, methoxyethane, has no O–H.

Any two of these ways to tell them apart:

  • ¹H NMR: propan-2-ol gives 3 peaks (6 : 1 : 1); propan-1-ol gives 4 peaks (3 : 2 : 2 : 1).
  • Mass spectrum: propan-2-ol shows m/z 45 (loss of CH3); propan-1-ol shows m/z 31 (CH2OH+, loss of C2H5).
  • Oxidation (acidified dichromate, then distil): propan-1-ol (primary) gives propanoic acid, an acidic product, while propan-2-ol (secondary) gives propanone.

(i) A is CH3CH2CH2COOH, butanoic acid.

(ii) B, C and D are neutral, sweet-smelling isomers, so they are esters.

• Butan-2-ol has a chiral carbon (C2), bonded to four different groups: H, OH, CH3 and C2H5.
  • Draw one enantiomer in 3-D (wedge/dash tetrahedral)…
  • …and its mirror image, clearly showing the mirror relationship.
  • Separate samples rotate plane-polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions.

(i) A (pentane) 36 °C; B (2-methylbutane) 28 °C; C (2,2-dimethylpropane) 10 °C. Reason: more branching gives a more compact/spherical molecule with less surface contact, so weaker London (dispersion) forces and a lower boiling point.

(ii) B: 2-methylbutane (methylbutane). C: 2,2-dimethylpropane (dimethylpropane). Not "2-dimethylpropane" or "2,2-methylpropane".

(i) cis: CH3 and CH2Cl on the same side of the C=C (H's on the other side); trans: CH3 and CH2Cl on opposite sides. (ClCH2–CH=CH–CH3.)

(ii) Rotation about the C=C double bond is restricted (the π bond would have to break), and each double-bond carbon has two different groups.

(iii) e.g. 3-chlorobut-1-ene, CH2=CH–C*HCl–CH3: the starred carbon carries four different groups (H, Cl, CH3, CH=CH2).

(i) The trans isomer (fumaric acid) has the higher melting point: its COOH groups are on opposite sides, so it forms (mainly) intermolecular hydrogen bonds between molecules; in the cis isomer (maleic acid) the COOH groups are close together and form (mainly) intramolecular hydrogen bonds, leaving weaker attractions between molecules.

(ii) The cis isomer readily loses water on gentle heating (forming a cyclic anhydride), because its two COOH groups are close together; the trans isomer does not.
A: 1-bromobutane; B: 2-bromobutane; C: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; D: 1-bromo-2-methylpropane. (2-bromomethylpropane and 1-bromomethylpropane accepted for C and D.)

• 2-bromobutane (B) – C2 is chiral (H, Br, CH3, C2H5).
  • Plane-polarized light is passed through a solution of each enantiomer in a polarimeter…
  • …the enantiomers rotate the plane of polarized light by equal amounts in opposite directions.
  • Physical properties are identical (except their effect on plane-polarized light).
  • Chemical properties are identical (except reactions with other chiral substances). "Similar" is not accepted.
Stereoisomers have the same structural formula (same atoms bonded in the same order) but a different arrangement of the atoms in space. ("Same molecular formula" alone is not enough.)

(i) A square cyclobutane ring with Cl on C1 and C3: cis-1,3-dichlorocyclobutane has both Cl atoms on the same side of the ring plane; trans-1,3-dichlorocyclobutane has them on opposite sides. Each mark needs structure + name.

(ii) The cis isomer has the higher boiling point: its C–Cl bond dipoles do not cancel, so it is polar, whereas in the trans isomer they cancel (non-polar). The cis isomer therefore has stronger (permanent) dipole–dipole forces between molecules.

The structure shown is trans (E)-but-2-ene, so the other isomer has both CH3 groups on the same side of the C=C: H(CH3)C=C(CH3)H with the CH3 groups cis. Name: cis-but-2-ene / (Z)-but-2-ene.

Why: the C=C cannot rotate, so the two arrangements are different compounds.
A cyclic isomer of C4H8: cyclobutane (a square ring of four CH2) or methylcyclopropane. These have no C=C, so they do not react with bromine water and it stays orange.

The chiral isomer is 2-bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3; C2 carries four different groups (H, Br, CH3, C2H5).

Draw two tetrahedral 3-D structures (wedges and dashes) that are mirror images of each other. They cannot be superimposed.

B is oxidized to a ketone C that resists further oxidation, so B is a secondary alcohol. E does not oxidize at all, so E is tertiary.

  • A: 2-chlorobutane, CH3CHClCH2CH3
  • B: butan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3
  • C: butanone, CH3COCH2CH3
  • D: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, (CH3)3CCl
  • E: 2-methylpropan-2-ol, (CH3)3COH

e.g. 2-bromopentane, CH3CHBrCH2CH2CH3. C2 is chiral, with four different groups: H, Br, CH3 and C3H7. Other acceptable isomers: 1-bromo-2-methylbutane or 2-bromo-3-methylbutane.

Draw the two enantiomers as 3-D tetrahedral structures (wedge and dash bonds) that are mirror images of each other. Marks: correct name, first 3-D structure, mirror-image structure.
